name: Access for Every Student
title: Access for Every Student
answer: Access for Every Student means using AI to make social studies, civics, and world languages content readable and understandable for all learners without lowering the intellectual demand. It matters because difficult texts, unfamiliar background knowledge, and language barriers can keep students on the edge of discussion instead of in it. The approach pairs leveled texts, glossaries, translations, background summaries, read aloud tools, and graphic organizers with teacher review and individualized education program team decisions.

crumbs.name: Social Studies, Civics, and World Languages

sections.body: Social studies reading is often dense, with long sentences, unfamiliar names, and abstract concepts. The leveled text approach from Chapter 6 lets a teacher present the same article, such as one on the causes of a war, at multiple reading levels while keeping and explaining key terms. The teacher then checks that the simpler versions did not erase important differences between causes, events, and consequences. English learners need both language support and background knowledge, so AI can help build short picture glossaries for terms like democracy, tariff, or migration and translate them into home languages. Background summaries can also support students who did not grow up with the history being taught, allowing them to join discussions rather than watch from the edge.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a classroom, a teacher can use AI to create several versions of the same social studies article at different reading levels, preserving and explaining key vocabulary. For English learners, the teacher can generate short glossaries with pictures for terms such as democracy, tariff, or migration and provide translations in students' home languages. Background summaries can be made for students who lack prior exposure to the history being taught. Students with disabilities can use text to speech through Microsoft Immersive Reader to hear documents read aloud, and AI generated graphic organizers can help them sort causes and effects. The text does not specify grade bands, so these practices are described across social studies, civics, and world languages rather than by grade level.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The supplied text gives no evidence label, study, figure, or finding for this idea. It describes a leveled text approach from Chapter 6 and practical supports such as glossaries, translations, background summaries, Microsoft Immersive Reader, and graphic organizers. Because no research evidence is stated, this idea rests on practice rather than research.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The teacher must check that simpler versions of a text did not blur important distinctions between causes, events, and consequences. The individualized education program team decides which supports fit each student, so that decision stays with people rather than with AI. Every support should open the content, not replace the thinking. English learners need both language and background knowledge, so supports should not be treated as a substitute for either. The text sets these limits to keep access connected to the actual intellectual work.
